According to Chinese media [and caught by Automaton Media], Shanghai police have arrested 13 individuals in connection to a bootleg toy operation, who oddly enough specialized in unlicensed dolls of Final Fantasy 7âs Tifa Lockhart.

Shanghai authorities began their investigation in May of this year. Purchasers of a figure based on Lockhartâs negligee appearance at the Honey Bee Inn were disappointed to discover what they received was not quite as advertised. While resembling the merchandise from Play Arts, Square Enixâs in-house toymaker, closer inspection revealed the goods were made of different material, had more simplistic attire and a lack of poseable articulation points. While some might shy away from flagging the cops about such specific buying habits, enough complaints came in to launch further inquiry.

Police have arrested 13 people accused of selling counterfeit Final Fantasy 7 Tifa Lockhart figures.

The Chinese sellers reportedly charged higher prices by including extra faces, hands, and accessories not found with the official figures pic.twitter.com/AE1IyS0wi9.

— Dexerto (@Dexerto) November 19, 2026.

In collaboration with the rights holders, police discovered an online network of unauthorized vendors using group chats and digital marketplaces to circulate the inauthentic merch. The ring of counterfeiters allegedly hired the services of a factory in Guangzhou to produce the goods. Police say the operation generated over 2 million yuan (approximately $300,000 USD) and had been selling the knock-offs since 2024. The 13 arrested had set up a front that even included a customer service rep.

Adding insult to injury, the forgeries were sold at a premium compared to the more inexpensive and legitimate article. Because they were unlicensed, the vendors apparently manufactured additional faces and accessories not sanctioned by Square Enix, though sadly they were left unspecified (letâs imagine itâs that cat sandwich NECAâs Alf came with). It is hardly an isolated incident. Like all recent collection frenzies, demand for upper-scale figurines of video game and anime characters has risen rapidly around the globe. GamesRadar says that this year alone, Shanghai police have arrested more than 140 individuals and confiscated over ten million dollars worth of bootleg play things.

Sources indicate that there are multiple endings to GTA 6, and not all the endings take place in the same location. One of the potential final scenes during the GTA 6 story mission, The End of the Road, takes place on a bridge in the Leonida Keys.

Recent findings suggest that after discovering the cops are onto them, Jason and Lucia drive away from Cal's house and head to Brian's marina to find an airplane. The police rapidly trap them on a bridge with a roadblock ahead and multiple cars behind them. Lucia wants to keep going but Jason thinks it's all over for them. The player is then given a choice, "Swim for it" or "No Surrender.".

It has been revealed that AGAIN, MASSIVE SPOILERS BELOW! STOP NOW IF YOU DON'T WANT TO KNOW THE ENDINGS!

Jason and Lucia decide Tomas is better off without them in his life. They drive through the roadblock, shooting at the cops. They're both shot to death and we see them dead in the front seat of the car, still holding hands. During the end credits, we see Tomas living happily with Lucia's sister and her husband and children.

Jason and Lucia decide to jump off the bridge and swim to freedom.

It has been revealed that however, a second choice appears once you've chosen 'Swim for it.' As Jason gets out of the car, a prompt for Lucia to 'Exit' the car appears. You can choose for Lucia to follow through with the strategy by pressing the button, or change your mind and let the prompt expire.

In a recent development, A: 'Swim for it' and 'Exit': The couple will get out of the car together and walk to the edge of the bridge. Lucia jumps but Jason does not, letting himself get arrested by the cops. During the credits, Lucia signs the deal which keeps her free and sends Jason to prison. We see her bring Tomas to visit him, so Jason finally meets his son, though it's through glass.

In a recent development, B: 'Swim for it' and don't 'Exit': If you choose to swim for it but don't choose the 'Exit' prompt, Jason will get out of the car but Lucia will remain in the car. The police will open fire and kill them both. As with the No Surrender option, we see Tomas living with Lucia's sister's family.

Recent findings suggest that C: 'Swim for it' and 'Exit' (with $2 million in Buck Me savings): If you delayed the Protective Custody mission of GTA 6 until you had deposited $2 million in savings, the Swim for it and Exit choices will show the same results, but during the credits, Lucia uses the money to get Jason released from prison. Lucia picks him up at prison, and Jason meets Tomas and holds his hand.

Industry observers note that note: These are not the only endings to GTA 6. I've seen several more endings that do not take place on the bridge at all and don't involve these particular choices.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tallulah Willis issued a public apology after sharing a rare new photo of her father, Bruce Willis, amid his frontotemporal dementia battle.

“Hi, I posted a photo of my dad yesterday because we were having a BEAUTIFUL visit,” Tallulah, 32, wrote via Instagram on Sunday, November 22, addressing her upload from the day prior. “I had someone take a super sweet photo of a shared moment between us watching a video of Frankie Valli singing.”.

Industry observers note that she continued, “I was very excited by the sweetness of the moment that I didn’t think farther ahead that this was possibly too intimate a photo to show. I can acknowledge that.”.

Tallulah shared a photo with Bruce, 71, on Saturday, November 21, in which they sat side-by-side on a porch with the caption, “🆒😎.” She has since deleted the post.

“[I] vow to do better,” she told her Instagram followers on Sunday. “I know you all love him. I love him, and he’s still always the absolute hero we know him to be.”.

Tallulah captioned her post, “I can do better.”.

Sources indicate that bruce shares Tallulah and sisters Rumer and Scout with ex-wife Demi Moore, in addition to younger daughters with wife Emma Heming Willis. The family announced in 2022 that Bruce was diagnosed with aphasia and, later, frontotemporal dementia that forced his four-decade storied Hollywood career to come to an end.

Bruce now lives apart from his family, and with a full-time care team, as he navigates life with his diagnosis.

“It was one of the hardest decisions that I’ve had to make so far,” Heming Willis, 50, mentioned in Emma and Bruce Willis: The Unexpected Journey – A Diane Sawyer Special, which aired in August 2025. “I knew, first and foremost, Bruce would want that for our daughters. You know, he would want them to be in a home that was more tailored to their needs, not his needs.”.

Throughout his health battle, his family has remained by his side. Bruce was even present during Tallulah’s wedding weekend this summer.

“A tender moment with my dad and Justin [Acee] at the start of wedding weekend,” she captioned a wedding photo shared with Vogue.

Check our latest news in Apple News.

Tallulah and Acee, 35, stated “I do” at the family’s Hailey, Idaho, residence in August.

“It’s the place where I learned to run free and be the dreamer that I am today,” Tallulah told Vogue of her ceremony venue. “Justin and I have spent so much time up there that even though it has such emotional pull for me, he feels very much a part of the fabric of the property. We toyed with the idea of making it simple and eloping, but deep down, I really loved the chance to be an eleganza.”.

#131534. ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Director Francis Lawrence on the Film’s Final Scene

‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Director Francis Lawrence on the Film’s Final Scene

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2417 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when Francis Lawrence, the filmmaker behind The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, greets me over Zoom, he’s aware that his darkly lit, gothic backdrop makes him look a bit like the villainous President Snow.
  • Lawrence has helmed almost every film in Lionsgate’s blockbuster series, based on Suzanne Collins’s best-selling novels about a dystopia where a bloodthirsty dictator forces children to fight to the death for the elite’s entertainment.
  • In a recent development, just as the original Hunger Games film made a star of Oscar winner Jennifer Lawrence (who returns for a scene in the upcoming movie), Sunrise on the Reaping introduces the world to Australian newcomer Joseph Zada.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when Francis Lawrence, the filmmaker behind The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, greets me over Zoom, he’s aware that his darkly lit, gothic backdrop makes him look a bit like the villainous President Snow. “All I need is a big eagle back here,” the white-haired, smartly dressed director jokes.

Lawrence has helmed almost every film in Lionsgate’s blockbuster series, based on Suzanne Collins’s best-selling novels about a dystopia where a bloodthirsty dictator forces children to fight to the death for the elite’s entertainment. He joined the franchise for its 2013 sequel, Catching Fire, and has directed only three non–Hunger Games movies in the decade-plus since. In that time, one could argue, the world has tilted further toward the oppressive future depicted in Collins’s novels—see, for instance, Donald Trump’s Hunger Games–esque Patriot Games. And while Lawrence isn’t naming names, he’s never lost sight of the movies’ larger political message. “I feel really lucky to be able to tell stories that matter, that are wrapped in these commercial packages,” he tells Vanity Fair. “So anytime one of these things comes around, I jump at it.”.

In a recent development, just as the original Hunger Games film made a star of Oscar winner Jennifer Lawrence (who returns for a scene in the upcoming movie), Sunrise on the Reaping introduces the world to Australian newcomer Joseph Zada. He plays the younger version of Woody Harrelson’s Haymitch Abernathy, a victor of the Hunger Games who later serves as a mentor to actor Lawrence’s Katniss Everdeen. Making a reflective movie prompted director Lawrence to reflect on his own Hollywood trajectory. “The biggest difference is that I’m a lot more relaxed. I was nervous as hell on Catching Fire,” he says. “It was my fourth movie. It was a movie I was inheriting. It was a major movie, and it was a massive cast. So I was really intimidated. Now I have much more fun, I will say. I’m much more comfortable with actors, and the amount of actors, and with logistics. And there’s definitely a family that’s built into it, which is very crucial for me. There’s, what, 14 years of my life spent making these movies? So it has to be fun.”.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: When did you become aware of Sunrise on the Reaping, and at what point did you and Suzanne Collins start discussing an adaptation?

Francis Lawrence: When we did the original series of movies, and we finished the last Mockingjay, she said she was done, and we thought that was it. Then she surprised me and Nina [Jacobson], the producer, with Ballad, however many years later. And she never tells us when she’s writing. Even when she has something to read, she never tells us what it’s about. She’s very superstitious about it all. So we got the call, which was very exciting. And she said, “Go to my agent’s house. There’s a manuscript. Let’s talk after you read it.”.

According to recent reports, I got to his house, sat in his backyard, and there was a manuscript and a copy of Catching Fire sitting on top of it with a few tabs in it. I opened to the tabs and saw that it had the portion where Katniss and Peeta were looking up the Haymitch Games, that sequence from the book. And I was like, Oh, she’s written the Haymitch story, which was very exciting. And that started the process that we always have, which is that I read the manuscript in one sitting, then read it a second time after having a conversation with Suzanne.

According to recent reports, then I fly to New York and meet her at Scholastic, and we sit up in a conference room for about a week going through the book, beat by beat, of what we think the movie is going to be. She and I lay it all out and chat, and she sits on her computer and writes a scriptment. Then that’s the thing that we turn over to the screenwriter.

How have you built that trust with the author of these books, having adapted them for more than a decade now?

It has been revealed that that working process happened accidentally when I signed on to do Catching Fire. I had never done a sequel to someone else’s first movie before. And when Lionsgate and the first director, [Gary Ross], parted ways and I got the call, they didn’t have a script, but they had started the process of developing it before I was on board. And so I signed on based on the book and had planned a trip to Newly introduced York to meet with Suzanne.

The script came on the day that I was traveling to Upcoming York. I read it, and it was not the movie that I wanted to make—because I loved the book, and it was not the book. Luckily, nobody else wanted to make that version of the movie either. Our meeting of me just picking her brain turned into, “This script doesn’t work. Let’s go through, page by page, and figure out the version of the movie we want to make.”.

Recent findings suggest that that’s what really formed the bond—just working really, really closely with her. Spending 8 or 10 hours a day for a week or two in a conference room—me riffing on visual ideas and her talking about the story. We think the same way in terms of storytelling, structure, and she seemed to take to my visual ideas.

There’s this weird dynamic that happens as we get closer to production. We’re usually developing the script pretty much within a week of shooting. But the production is also building. So you have thousands of people working, figuring out locations, traveling in different parts of the world. The stress levels are building.

In a recent development, suzanne and I have related the relationship to almost like a mother-son relationship. It starts really lovely and creative, but then as we get closer and closer, it’s me being that late teen who’s ready to leave the home, like, Okay, enough’s enough. I’m going to go make the movie now. I have to say, I love the process. It’s not without its stress sometimes, but that’s part of the closeness of it all that I cherish.

How did this film’s futuristic-meets-1970s aesthetic come about?

In a recent development, there was an element [of the story] that reminded me a bit of Alice in Wonderland, which then made me think of Jefferson Airplane, that song “White Rabbit,” which brought me to the ’60s and ’70s. Then you can look at characters certain ways. Like, Haymitch, you go, Okay, he’s from, like, young Bruce Springsteen, or Lenore Dove [played by Whitney Peak], like a young Stevie Nicks. And you get this hippie vibe. And the Capitol is that Warhol Studio 54 crowd, and Snow like a ’70s Yves Saint Laurent.

How do you go about casting a young Haymitch, finding an actor who can anchor the film like Jennifer Lawrence did in the original Hunger Games film?

In a recent development, our casting director, Deb Zane, had met him, and I want to say before he did East of Eden. She had a lot of faith in him. We liked his self-tape a lot. But we knew that he was going to have to pull a lot off. He starts as a very optimistic, fun, playful, young guy in love, and in this movie has to turn into somebody that’s much closer to the Haymitch that we’re used to—cynical and a drunk. He’s going to have to go through a lot of emotional trauma, plus have that kind of mischievousness, irreverence, all these different elements that Woody [Harrelson] has naturally. And so we really put him through the ringer. We did a lot of tests, kept bringing him back, bringing him back, bringing him back. He and I were modulating how much Woody we feel in his performance.

In a recent development, I want to make sure that everybody makes the role their own. That they find the spirit of the character and that it’s not trying to do an imitation of somebody. That’s true of Elle [Fanning] doing Effie, of Ralph [Fiennes] doing Snow, of Jesse [Plemons] doing Plutarch, Kieran [Culkin] as Caesar. Everybody has to figure out how to do it on their own. Then the weird thing is that Kelvin [Harrison Jr., who plays a young Beetee], has worked with Jeffrey [Wright] three times. So he’s fairly close with Jeffrey. When he got the role, he called and stated, “You won’t believe this, but I’m actually playing the young version of you.” He could just conjure Jeffrey Wright. His voice, the speech patterns, the timbre of the sound of everything. It was pretty wild.

It has been revealed that were there storylines from the previous films that you felt you could plant Easter eggs for? I’m thinking specifically of the romantic chemistry between Effie and Haymitch.

There are certain Capitol characters where I give a lot of freedom for improvisation. Effie, Caesar, Drusilla [played by Glenn Close], there’s a lot of room for ad-libs. One of the elements that we definitely played with a bit came from an improvised moment in the [last] Mockingjay. We were shooting this scene in Atlanta outside of Snow’s mansion, which is one of the very last scenes of Katniss in the Capitol. She’s saying goodbye to Effie, and then Haymitch and Effie kiss.

Industry observers note that quite honestly, it was an idea because Woody just wanted to kiss Elizabeth Banks. But everybody thought it would be fun and that the fans would dig it, that Haymitch kissed her. Then it became this significant thing of this hidden love that Haymitch and Effie have for one another. And Elle played into that a bit. So there’s, I would say, a hint of flirtation here between the two, less so on Haymitch’s side. His heart is obviously somewhere else in the story. But Elle definitely brought a bit of that to it. That was not scripted. That’s the fun of having great actors.

What was it like to reunite Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson from the original movies?

Jen and I have stayed close over the years. We’ve done four movies together. Josh, who basically has moved to Spain, I haven’t seen in a long time. Woody I see off and on and text every once in a while. But there was something really special about the three of them being back together.

It has been revealed that it’s also really, for the most part, the same crew from 2012, when we started making Catching Fire. It’s the same DP [Jo Willems], the same camera operator [David J. Thompson], the same AD [Christopher Surgent].

Sources indicate that [When] they got to the hotel, Jen and Josh were in the bar having a beer or something, and I was like, Okay, I won’t even shower. I won’t get out of my rain gear. I’ll just come in. The next thing you know, there were 40 of us who had been together since Catching Fire, the gang back together. It’s like a high school reunion or something, but in the best possible way.

There’s a futility to what happens in this film, knowing where we end up in future movies. How do you handle that aspect of history being doomed to repeat itself?

It has been revealed that look, we’re doing a story where you know the lead character is going to make it out. It’s really about how he makes it out, and what he ends up being like at the end of it all. What I’m really pleased about is that the way Suzanne wrote the book, and the way I think we’ve ended the movie, there is a sense of hope that the tragedy is not for nothing. That was really vital to me. And one of the beautiful elements in the story, which comes a bit later, is this sense of, everybody has to find their voice. Everybody has to participate.

It really deals with this thing that I think is happening a lot today, where you find apathy: people not wanting to vote, feeling even if they do vote that it’s not going to matter. This idea that you have to be active, and you can’t expect immediate gratification—that everybody needs to stand up and it may take generations, but you still have to do it.

Outside of my screening on the Upper West Side, there was a group protesting Elon Musk and data centers because the documentary about him was playing at the theater. It was a reminder that there will always be something to rise up against, and always people who will be willing to do it.

Yeah, exactly. And ideally, at some point, if everybody stands up, something will change.

During the 13 years that you’ve worked in this universe, dystopia has felt more and more familiar. How have real-world events influenced your filmmaking?

In the 56 years I’ve been alive, there’s never really been a time where I’ve felt like, Oh wow, everything is great. Nothing is wrong in the world. It always feels like there’s some dystopian sense about the world at any given time. And somehow Suzanne is always able to write these stories about it, which is what makes these movies feel timeless. A lot of people just see them as spectacles, but really they’re about our times very specifically. Almost in a subversive way, I feel like we’ve gotten to smuggle these ideas into these movies that a lot of people go see.

The Epic Games Store continues to give away a free game each week, and this week's offering is another nice find at a price that can't be beat. Every Thursday at 8 AM PT / 11 AM ET, Epic offers at least one free PC game (and sometimes even as many as two or three). All you need to do to claim the free games is create a free Epic account and enable two-factor authentication. You have a week to add the freebies to your library before the latest one(s) take their place. At this point, Epic has given away hundreds of free games, and there's no sign that the program will stop any time soon. The firm has also extended its freebies to Android devices, and you can claim a free game every week here as well. We keep this article up to date weekly to highlight both the current free games and next week's offerings.

If you're looking for more freebies, you can check out our list of the 25 best free PC games to play right now, or for more options, the 25 best free games to play on multiple platforms.

This week's free game is Mark of the Deep, a 2025 pirate-themed adventure with a mix of Metroidvania and soulslike gameplay.

Next week, you can get a welcome gift pack for Firestone: Idle Clicker Online RPG, and you can help a pair of penguins out in the co-op platformer Bread & Fred.

We're keeping a running list of every free game that Epic people have been able to claim in the past. From AAA hits to indie darlings, Epic has really made its mark with free games. You can even snag these games if you don't have a powerful PC so you can play them if you ever get one. Look at the list below to see the frankly ridiculous list of free games that have been available.

Tech Report: There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage.
  • That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public.
  • It has been revealed that but to skeptics of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication challenges." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen.".

It has been revealed that but to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Sources indicate that love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering newly introduced security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

According to recent reports, mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find latest security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be remarked for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

Industry observers note that you might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October enhancement. The tech giant's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It has been revealed that it's notable to understand that just about every organization that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as swiftly as possible.

Recent findings suggest that the implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

Industry observers note that earlier today, however, Reddit user ShweetsStuff posted a comprehensive breakdown of the new music tracks alleging they were made with Suno, an AI-based music generation tool. “The new update includes 14 music files for the run; seven full songs, plus some derivatives (intros/outros),” the wrote. 💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that over the last couple of weeks, some Nvidia users noticed their SSDs were taking a hammering, reporting their driver's log file was being overwritten constantly, sometimes to the tune of 30 GB every hour. Which obviously isn't great for the lifespan of the valuable SSD you've got it installed on.

Given the problem was caused by recent driver updates, rolling back to version 621.01 was the best solution until Nvidia could do something about it. Which they did, releasing a hotfix as version 621.35. It's not available in the GeForce app yet, but you can download it directly from Nvidia's site. Not that you should.

As customers on the Nvidia subreddit are reporting, the problem persists. While the hotfix reduces the peak write rate and prevents it for a short while after reboot, it eventually creeps back in. One user reported that overnight the log file was still being rewritten by approximately 4.5 GB every hour.

Sources indicate that so yeah, the best solution remains to roll back to version 621.01 and, as always with Nvidia drivers, to hold off on updating to the latest driver until it's been confirmed safe. If this ongoing saga sounds familiar, it's because the same thing happened to AMD's GPU drivers earlier this month. Maybe vibecoding driver updates and then vibecoding fixes for their inevitable bugs isn't the best way of doing things.

  • It has been revealed that when people want to know how bad the economics are in California, and Los Angeles in particular in terms of the industry that created this town.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I knew it had become increasingly rare for Hollywood productions to actually be filmed in Los Angeles, but Rob Lowe’s stats for The Floor really put things into perspective. The host of the Fox game show, which is on the 2026 TV schedule this fall season, just got real about why it’s filmed all the way in Ireland rather than at the network’s own lot. And, wow!

Sources indicate that ever since The Floor premiered back in 2023, the game show featuring 100 contestants, a giant LED floor grid and a $250,000 grand prize has been made in Ireland. When Lowe was asked why he shoots it overseas, he stated this:.

It has been revealed that when people want to know how bad the economics are in California, and Los Angeles in particular in terms of the industry that created this town. It is more cost-efficient to find 100 Americans and bring them to Ireland and shoot the game show in Ireland than it is to shoot in the soundstages [on the Fox lot] right outside the window of the offices where we’re trying to figure out what we’re going to do next season.

Yeah, this really illustrates the rough situation in LA right now. When I looked deeper into it, I found out that there are a few factors that probably played into The Floor deciding to go to Ireland rather than stay in Los Angeles. One is the rigid labor regulations in Los Angeles that just don’t apply in Ireland. Another is how much more expensive it would be for the production to board the one hundred contestants during the shoots. And then, there’s the competitive tax incentives Ireland has in place to encourage productions to be there. Lowe continued with these words:.

In a recent development, there’s a upcoming California initiative that did pass to help bring production back into LA. And then, there's also a national one that people are talking about. But, that would still only make it competitive with some of the other [markets]. I mean, it’s 40% less expensive, 40. It’s a lot of money.

According to recent reports, it sounds like The Floor just wouldn’t be able to exist if it were shot in Los Angeles. There are a number of TV shows that at the moment shoot in the City of Angels, like Dancing With The Stars, The Pitt, The Rookie, 911, Shrinking and Abbott Elementary, and some incentives in California are starting to help repair the market. However, as Lowe also shared while on Mostly Sheenius, there’s a long way to go before it becomes cost-efficient again. As he put it:.

It is definitely trending up, but it is trending up from the basement of where it used to be.

Tons of Los Angeles TV shows recently moved to upcoming locations, such as Shark Tank and American Idol moving to Atlanta and The Masked Singer to New Jersey. It’s also been reported lately (per Deadline) that America’s Got Talent is scouting a new home outside of its longtime home in Pasadena, California.

In a recent development, the Floor airs new episodes on Wednesdays (with the finale airing on December 2). If you’re looking to catch up on the new season, you can do so now with either a Disney+ subscription and/or a Hulu subscription. Lowe’s explanation of why The Floor shoots in Ireland kind of blows my mind, but as a Los Angeles resident, I totally see how expensive it is over here, too. Hopefully some of these incentives will change things because so much of the workforce over here relies on the entertainment industry.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Sarah El-Mahmoud has been with CinemaBlend since 2018 after graduating from Cal State Fullerton with a degree in Journalism. In college, she was the Managing Editor of the award-winning college paper, The Daily Titan, where she specialized in writing/editing long-form features, profiles and arts & entertainment coverage, including her first run-in with movie reporting, with a phone interview with Guillermo del Toro for Best Picture winner, The Shape of Water. Now she's into covering YA television and movies, and plenty of horror. Word webslinger. All her writing should be read in Sarah Connor’s Terminator 2 voice over.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto 6 has plenty of famous faces and voices behind its many, many characters.
  • According to recent reports, grand Theft Auto 6 has plenty of famous faces and voices behind its many, many characters.
  • In one of the later missions, players accompany Boobie on one of his errands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6 has plenty of famous faces and voices behind its many, many characters. From Bobby Moynihan as your verbose bestie to Weird Al Yankovic as a radio host, there's plenty of star power here--and you can even spot an influential figure from GTA history making a quick cameo. Spoilers below Who could it be now? In one of the later missions, players accompany Boobie on one of his errands. Once they reach a newly introduced club, Boobie meets up with Major Mike and throws a few jibes at the local help sweeping the floor. That "little Santa" with the broom? None other than Rockstar Games president Sam Houser, who doesn't speak a single word in his brief appearance. As an added touch, Houser's digital doppelganger wears a white t-shirt with the Rockstar Games logo. Because the thumbnail for it is a big ol' spoiler, you can click this link to see the Houser cameo for yourself. This isn't the first time that Houser has cameoed in one of his studio's games. In GTA 3, he voiced one of the Ammu-Nation store clerks, and in GTA: San Andreas, a statue of that Ammu-Nation employee could be found in the game's Downtown Square area. Beyond minor background pedestrian and gangster voice roles in San Andreas and GTA 4, Houser has generally kept a low profile, focusing instead on developing the studio's games. With GTA 6 launching to major critical and commercial success, Houser has also issued a rare statement to mark the occasion. "This is a narrative set in a world of possibilities--and it is up to you as the player to shape how it ultimately feels and concludes," he said. Meanwhile, Houser's brother, Dan Houser, is working on an open-world comedy game at Absurd Ventures, the studio he founded after leaving Rockstar Games in 2020. For more on GTA 6, check out GameSpot's Grand Theft Auto 6 guides hub for tips, tricks, and walkthroughs.

Hasan Piker Joins VF’s Fair Game: “I Am Not a Terrorist”

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 51 min read (10111 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the most prominent figures of the so-called Bluenami was not a candidate on the ballot, but rather a Twitch streamer and political commentator: Hasan Piker.
  • In a recent development, this year Hasan was involved in dozens of races across the country, campaigning for progressive candidates like Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed.
  • According to recent reports, hasan regularly courts controversy on both his hours-long Twitch streams, where he’s said things like “America deserved 9/11,” and social media, where he’s written that Hamas “is a thousand times better than” Israel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the most prominent figures of the so-called Bluenami was not a candidate on the ballot, but rather a Twitch streamer and political commentator: Hasan Piker.

In a recent development, this year Hasan was involved in dozens of races across the country, campaigning for progressive candidates like Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed. But you’re probably more likely to associate Hasan’s name with what other people have had to say about him—from Fox News commentators to more established members of the Democratic Party.

According to recent reports, hasan regularly courts controversy on both his hours-long Twitch streams, where he’s said things like “America deserved 9/11,” and social media, where he’s written that Hamas “is a thousand times better than” Israel. He claims he’s often taken out of context, and that his audience knows what he really means—and where he stands. In his mind, he’s a leftist provocateur, maybe, but one who understands the importance of working-class values and electoral strategy.

Recent findings suggest that while Hasan has walked back some of his more inflammatory language, his rhetoric raises the question: Is he a liability to the cause he champions? Or is he successfully reaching the critical audience—namely, young men—that helped elect the wave of progressives poised to take office in January?

With 2028 on the horizon, I wanted to know how Hasan thinks about his growing platform, and if he sees his role shifting in the media landscape. What responsibility does he have to his viewers and to the candidates he supports? And does he regret any of those past statements?

We also got into the DSA’s more extreme positions and how to make sense of them; why he thinks the Republicans put his thirst trap on the jumbotron at their convention; and how he, a self-proclaimed socialist, thinks about his own money.

Mark Guiducci: Hasan Piker, welcome to Fair Game.

Hasan Piker: Very excited to be here.

Sources indicate that thanks for coming. Hasan, you are more online than just about anyone. You spend at least seven hours a day streaming. You reach tens of thousands of people at a time on average, and it’s all in the channel that you control. I’m curious, what are you doing here with me today? Why are you showing up for a show with a legacy media publication? What’s in it for you?

In a recent development, well, I saw the clips and everybody looked really good. The lighting was perfect. I saw the Dari[aliza Avila Chevalier] clips, I saw Ta-Nehisi [Coates], and I was like, I got to get in on that.

Sources indicate that yeah. So shouts out to the team. You guys did a phenomenal job lighting this up. It looks very cool too.

Industry observers note that okay. We’ll take the compliment.

Sources indicate that but the serious answer is, I mean, I reach an audience that obviously does not watch television, does not read legacy publications at all. And I want to show people that read Vanity Fair that I am not a terrorist.

Right. Which brings me to my next question because—.

Industry observers note that yeah, exactly. That would be the name of the episode. You’ve been everywhere this year, and you became this kind of bogeyman for the right, who probably have never heard you, watched your stream, or heard anything you’ve said out of your mouth. They’ve just heard quotes repeated by news anchors. And not even just for the right, even for some on the left. And you played this interesting role because you were a surrogate and a media figure and then a media figure covering the media as well. I want to spend a little bit of time talking about how you see your role. And to start, do you consider yourself a journalist?

In a recent development, okay. Because it’s like you present this interesting new type of figure. I was thinking about how you’ve done an interview with CNN, you’ve done interviews with MS NOW, but they don’t have you on as much as I would expect them to.

I have some thoughts, but I wonder why you think that is.

I think I’ve pissed off a bunch of executives over there, because, in my experience, there are plenty of amazing reporters and journalists and producers that I know that work at all of these newsrooms, right? But from what I have seen, the masthead has a very different editorial slant than sometimes what the reporters want to cover.

Because they talk about you a lot.

They talk about me a lot. And also I’ve never been invited on any of these outlets as a pundit either, which is also strange because, as you also pointed to, I don’t just operate as a campaignster. As a matter of fact, that’s something I did very briefly and I did not like it at all. I’m first and foremost a commentator…. I do have the capacity to do journalism at times. I’ll do interviews with candidates. I’ll go out and—.

Well, candidates I like. Sometimes I do interviews with candidates I don’t like or I’m unsure about as well. The problem is most of the candidates don’t want to come on if they know I’m gonna cook ’em. Like Gavin Newsom, I have had feelers out to get him on the broadcast.

Industry observers note that I have. Gavin, Gavin, come on the show. I am a taxpaying California resident. I’m one of your constituents. You want to be president in 2028, you’re gonna have to be able to talk to people like myself.

All right. So, Hasan, this cycle you were involved in some way in, by one count, 48 different candidates’ races, and AIPAC and pro-Israel groups spent about $101 million in those races. And on Election Day, your stream was the second most watched in the country after NBC News’s “Kornacki Cam.” With a little bit of distance, how are you thinking about what happened a couple of weeks ago, both for yourself and for the country?

Recent findings suggest that I feel a lot of hope. Hopefully it’s not going to be short-lived. But I feel very excited for the first time in a very long time, after 10 years of some of the most odious politics that we’ve seen from Trumpism, from MAGA. We finally saw a real sea change through electoralism. People truly have had enough with Trumpism.

Sources indicate that I wouldn’t be so certain because I feel like if there’s one controlled opposition party that is capable of breathing life back into MAGA, it would be the establishment Democrats. So I’m a little bit worried, but it’s very clear that people are truly fed up.

All right. So there are a couple of different narratives that are coming out of the midterms right now. Rahm Emanuel, for instance, is touting this as a victory for moderate Democrats, saying that they ran 21 points above Kamala Harris. The DSA, meanwhile, is claiming that American voters have “emphatically endorsed socialism.” Other pundits are saying that these major gains have nothing to do with the Democrats and are actually about the war in Iran and high gas prices. So does this debate between moderates and progressives feel like a healthy back-and-forth to you, or does this feel like the upcoming aisle that has to be straddled?

I mean, I think this is not even a upcoming debate. This factional battle has existed within the Democratic Party and perhaps—.

Yeah, but the progressive wing was always really fringe.

Recent findings suggest that and now we’re talking about—I don’t know if 50/50 is right. I don’t want to use numbers, but—.

I think it’s a testament to our success, especially in the midterms, that there are a lot of people who are trying to protect their comfortable sinecures and are outright panicking. And all of that completely sidesteps the reality that the vulgar Bernie-ism of 2016 was echoed through every single candidacy, every single campaign all across the country, from the obvious Berniecrats like Abdul El-Sayed to even people like Roy Cooper, who in the past were very moderate, very centrist. And he still is a center-right figure, which clearly works in North Carolina. But even he was railing against data centers, billionaires, the uncertainty surrounding AI. I mean, this is left populism. And that rhetoric, one could say, was deployed in the past by even the likes of Bill Clinton and Al Gore.

Recent findings suggest that but for some strange reason, there was a turning point in 2016 where the Democratic Party adopted this strange role of defending the corporate class and defending the elites and took ownership over, I guess, defending these institutions overall. And these institutions are worthy of defending, for the record. However, from the perspective of the masses, if the government is failing them, if these institutions are failing them, then they wanted someone to break it. And that was obviously the right populism of Donald Trump. And break those institutions, he surely did. And we’ve seen the devastating results of that.

So you credit the progressivism with what happened on election night?

Absolutely. I mean, there’s certainly local moderation on challenges, right? Because James Talarico went from saying “God is nonbinary” to “we need to defend our transgender brothers and sisters, our neighbors,” which is, again, insanely woke for Texas, or just in general, right? There are far more conservative figures in the party than James Talarico’s current position on the trans issue.

Okay. But sometimes the way that you run—oftentimes the way that you run needs to be different than the way that you govern or lead once you’re there. Do you think it is productive to continue pushing some of the farther-left ideas once they get to Congress? Or is pragmatism and getting things done, you know, defining things that are really achievable and sticking to them as a bloc, as a group, and pushing them over the line— when you’re talking to some of these winners, are you talking about [that]?

I think if I could speak to the entire incoming freshman class or the entire caucus—.

According to recent reports, I would say, be bold, be brave, and obviously immediately implement accountability. Investigations are an absolute must. This is what people are demanding. After the economy, the second concern, the biggest concern, is corruption. The second term with Trump has been unbelievable. I mean, look, I’m Turkish. I’ve seen corruption in the Turkish government. I’ve seen corruption and tracked it and talked about it all around the world with different governments. I’ve never seen anything like what the Trump administration has done because of how flagrant and in your face it was. And I think people responded to that, finally, in the appropriate way they should, with anger.

So you’re calling for subpoenas and investigations.

I think impeachment, especially for Trump, is probably the last thing that I care about. I mean, I want these guys to go to jail. Let’s be clear. If they’ve done the crime, they need to do the time. I don’t think anyone is above the law. We have to restore law and order. So I’m a law-and-order Democrat. And I know that sounds something very different in Washington, DC, or in general. I think when politicians say that, they mean, like, punish the poor for minor crimes. I’m talking about punishing the wealthy for their corruption, for their major crimes, because they’re the ones who are robbing people blind.

But, you know, a lot of people would say that impeachment would be a distraction. So I guess what I’m saying is, if you had to choose three agenda items that the Democrats are agreeing on and they’re going forward with—you already said subpoenas and investigations.

Sources indicate that what else? What are the other two that in the first year you really want to see happen?

Recent findings suggest that I think it’s virtually impossible [with] the current DOJ to—they’re not impartial, right? I don’t think that we are going to move the needle on actual criminal investigations before the Democrats win the White House in 2028. But all of this is building up for that moment. And for that reason, I think we need to talk about affordability—and not just simply talk about affordability, but also explain how we’re going to solve the affordability crisis through a comprehensive legislative agenda. And one of the major issues around affordability that is oftentimes discussed as a separate thing, but it’s not, is health care. And the Democratic Party’s approach to health care has been lackluster. Even though Americans obviously overwhelmingly trust the Democrats with fixing health care or solving the problem with health care, the reality of the matter is, while the ACA was a fantastic improvement to what existed previously, it’s not enough, and we have to move the needle in a healthier direction. We have to push for a single-payer health care solution.

Sources indicate that I’m perfectly fine with that. I’ve joked about that for years ’cause he’s so invested. He’s such a petty despot and so narcissistic that—.

Industry observers note that yes. I have pitched this over and over again on my show. Look, you win so major with Donald Trump if you go to Donald Trump and you say, “Look, Obamacare, not the best, right? Now you get to destroy Obamacare and you get to build something else in your name. We call it Trumpcare. It’s single-payer. It’s Medicare for All.” I think he would do it.

Look at this. Bipartisan collaboration.

According to recent reports, yes, I’m pragmatic. I’m bipartisan.

Industry observers note that all right, so let’s take a step back. You were talking a second ago about how Talarico was woke. And on November 4, Twitter, formerly known as X, was amazing. Memes, jokes, you know.

I see what you did there. Yeah. We flipped it back.

Yeah, we flipped it back. With the Democrats’ victory, the idea that woke was back, do you think that’s true? Do you think that we’re going to see, culturally, the return of this idea of woke? And do you think that’s a good thing for the Democrats?

Yes. I do think that the pendulum swing was an inevitability. I talked about this quite a bit. I saw the early warning signs when [Joe] Biden won. That was one of my major warnings that young men were going to go back to the Gamergate era of very far-right politics because the Biden administration was not delivering. And what ended up happening with this anti-woke narrative, this culture war that the Republicans had seemingly won, that they presented as a mandate, right, was some of the most odious commentary, some of the most vile rhetoric that anyone had ever seen.

Definitely. The idea of woke now, though, I'm just curious—being politically correct or precise in one’s language was, for a time, an outward indication of being a progressive or maybe even being a good person in culture. Do you think that’s still the case?

I mean, I’m progressive, so I think so, but I’m a little biased. But I will say this: I think that there were certainly social excesses, which is ironic because this whole Woke 1.0, 2.0 distinction, I feel a little responsible for in the discourse because I jokingly used to say—.

Yeah, now I’ve joked about that too, and now journalists are reaching out to me being like, “Do you think Woke 3.0 is real?” I’m like, “I’m joking, guys. It’s not serious.” But here’s the thing, there is a little bit of sincerity there. I think one of the things that I routinely criticized during that 2016-to-2022, 2023, era of, I guess, Woke 1.0 was the social excesses, the maximalist demands, the inability to understand that people are complex and don’t have the same lived experience that everybody else has. I always would get so frustrated because we on the left say America’s a white supremacist country, and yet we don’t ever reflect on what kind of social conditioning comes along with that. So that if you do actually hear someone engage in a microaggression, for example, that we have to be a little bit more understanding and try to ease them into the conversation.

In a recent development, and on the other side, people will say, “Oh, that’s normalizing this kind of behavior. It’s unacceptable.” And I totally see the other side of that argument as well, but I think, especially if you’re campaigning or especially if you’re building a movement, you do have to be a little bit more understanding and not be so hardheaded and assume that everyone has to agree with you from the jump without you making a convincing case as to why you might be correct.

In a recent development, okay. All right. So we’ve talked a lot about what you think about the political landscape, but I want to talk also about your role in it right now and going forward. So initially, you were called the Joe Rogan of the left. Recently, you’ve said you operate more like a Charlie Kirk. Is that the right analog for the kind of influence you want to have? And if not, is there another?

Industry observers note that I don’t think there is an appropriate analog because I’m everything all at once at the same time, because I work out and I do collaborations with people who are not expressly political, so that’s kind of like Joe Rogan. I go out and operate sometimes as a campaign surrogate, and I do rallies at college campuses and I deliver speeches, so that’s kind of like Charlie Kirk. But then usually my day-to-day commentary is what I like to jokingly refer to as a Rush Limbaugh for Zoomers. So I do all of those things at the same time, and that’s, I think, part of the reason why it’s so hard to make sense of what I do from the perspective of someone who just doesn’t understand Twitch or doesn’t understand exactly what I’m doing and has only seen negatively framed clips or clips out of context, that kind of thing. Having stated that, on the political-ideological side of things, of course I am the furthest from all of those figures. I’m just talking about the form and function of it all.

Industry observers note that okay. So it seems like you’ve been recently the guy that progressives come to when they’re trying to run a primary from the left, but then when they get to the general or to office, maybe they don’t need you as much, or they have left you behind, or they distanced themselves from you. And I think about [Zohran] Mamdani in this case. I just—.

Maybe because of that Rush Limbaugh–esque heightened rhetoric; do you agree with that characterization? And how does that make you feel?

Well, my feelings are immaterial in this. As long as they’re delivering, I think that’s what matters. I’ve noted this before: I love Zohran and, off the rip, my attitude on this was always just put the policies in the bag. If you’re delivering for the people of Upcoming York, and if you’re delivering successfully and every success that you have as a democratic socialist mayor of New York bodes well for the rest of this movement, then I’m happy.

Yeah, but are you talking to him behind the scenes? There’s still a relationship there? Because honestly—.

Yes. But the thing is, what I’m doing is too latest for people to fully realize, to fully comprehend. So of course there’s going to be some growing pains as far as how to navigate through an unbelievably contentious media environment, especially if the candidate[s] themselves are Muslim. And, you know, I think that is the reason why—the two major figures that I can point to that have done a little bit of distancing, at least in rhetoric, even though they never disavow the platform, disavow the person, they just say, “Oh, I don’t agree with that statement”—those two figures are Abdul El-Sayed and Zohran Mamdani. They’re both very progressive. One’s a democratic socialist, the other one’s not, but they’re still very progressive for American politics, and they’re Muslim. I think that is a significant part of the reason why I’ve given them a lot more bandwidth to operate in this space in whichever way they want to, because the expectation or the fears that they have are very real. As someone who has been at the center of a lot of this manufactured outrage, a lot of this controversy, being presented as an Islamist, jihadist at times, a terrorist, I know the role that the first Muslim senator has to play on the campaign trail. So on that front, of course they got to do what they got to do.

So you intellectually understand it, but do you feel used?

In a recent development, I would only feel that way if they did not follow through on their promises that they made on the campaign trail. If Abdul came out tomorrow and was like, “Money out of politics? Maybe money in politics. Money in your pocket? Maybe you don’t get money in your pocket. Medicare for All? Medicare for some”—if he were to just flip the script on not just me, but Michiganders and America as a whole, then I would feel very betrayed.

Sources indicate that so we talked a little bit earlier about your audience at the very beginning. You know, you’re an interesting figure for them. There are a significant number of them that are with you for hours on end a day, and I think they probably look up to you. What responsibility do you feel to the people who watch your streams?

Industry observers note that as far as the responsibilities that I have, I am very aware of them. I see myself as, in some respects, NPR for Zoomers. For many people, and now even an older audience as well, I am their primary news outlet. They have me on in the background, and I’m offering news and commentary throughout the day while they’re going through and doing their chores or at work with me blasting in one ear. So I know that if I were to stop randomly, people would feel it, because I see it as—I listen to The Daily; I listen to NPR every morning. If somehow I wake up one morning and NPR is no longer on, I’d be like, What happened? How am I gonna figure out what’s going on in the world?

Yeah, that’s just a lot of pressure, though, because NPR has a whole staff of people that, [if] someone’s sick, someone can pinch-hit.

I mean, I’m fine living in that environment. I’m happy to do it. I’m happy to take on that responsibility.

Can I ask, what’s your personal life like right now? I mean, that is a lot of time on the air, and probably you have to read the news yourself too. So are you seeing friends a lot? Do you see your family a lot?

I keep my private life private for obvious reasons ’cause there are a lot of insane people out there. But yes, I do spend a good deal of time with friends and family. I have normie friends as well that are just completely removed from the world of politics and from the world of Hollywood, influencers, that kind of thing.

Yeah, no, they keep me grounded, for sure, and my family certainly does as well. I spend every waking moment that I’m not on camera doing things like that, you know, enjoying the finer things in life.

Do you think of yourself as a role model?

It has been revealed that in some respects, yes. I don’t think people should follow everything that I do to a T, but I definitely do see that. I recognize the responsibility that influencers have over so many people, and I try to put my best foot forward in an effort to cultivate a nicer space on the internet, one that is more productive for people. I try to urge people to go out and unionize in their workplaces, join the Democratic Socialists of America, but then also at the same time, I try to get them to go out and work out. I’m very open about my fitness journey, my health journey. And the same even goes for my presentation. I’ve gone through these different eras now on my broadcast. Right now we’re in the suit arc. And then I sometimes see that reflected in the crowd as well when I go out to these rallies. I start seeing people also wearing suits, which is a little strange to experience, but it’s not the worst thing, right?

I think that’s a good influence.

Yeah, I think that is a good influence. You’re rocking a nice suit yourself.

According to recent reports, I bought this at a photo shoot for Days magazine. This stylist had pulled this and I loved it.

I literally was like, “I’m buying this from you.” And then since then, she’s been pulling stuff for me.

Sources indicate that can I ask, are you having fun? Because it seems like you are, but then what we were talking about before, with the way that you might feel abandoned—and especially the past few months, this cycle, has it been fun?

It has been revealed that no, it has not been fun. I don’t think it’s great to be called a terrorist and lied about and slandered endlessly with the hopes that this could potentially tank the Democratic Party’s chances of bringing about accountability to this fascist administration. I did not enjoy that.

It has been revealed that and I certainly also did not enjoy the fact that I was kind of left out on my own a little bit, where—of course I got a lot of support from the movement, DSA, and the wonderful slate of candidates that we worked with, but I’ve never had institutional backing. And as a matter of fact, there was a lot of anxiety from the institution that is the Democratic Party. So all of its loyal servants were going on TV and being like, “He’s a horrible person who needs to go away,” over and over again. So that didn’t feel great. ’Cause there’s always negative polarization when Trump attacks someone and the Republicans attack someone, but if there isn’t any backing from the liberal side, even from a partisan perspective, then that complicates things. All of a sudden you’re like, Okay, well, who’s on my side now? I have nobody to push back.

Sources indicate that you’re playing this game where you try to find the worst quotes that you can and frame them as negatively as you can, and then attack candidates that might not even know the context behind some of these words. Bernie was, I think, the best, ironically enough, at dealing with it when he was asked by Abby Phillip. He called me a radio man, which is funny. He’s been on the show, still doesn’t know what I do, which is fine. That’s unc, that’s grand-unc. But he basically remarked, “Look, everybody states silly things. I mean, he talks for thousands of hours. He’s a radio man. And not only does everybody say silly things, but ultimately there’s a reason why he has such a passionate fan base, because we agree on the broad spectrum of complications that he advocates for, and so do all of his fans. So to reduce someone to a couple of choice clips is obviously going to never give you the full picture.” I mean, he didn’t use all those words.

It’s not about being a person; it’s about being a cudgel, just something that you can use as a counterbalance.

According to recent reports, I don’t think liberals, and even the left broadly, [are] ready for how to deal with that because we’ve never really had a person like me in the past. I mean, the Republicans obviously have three to four decades of this, coming from William F. Buckley all the way to Rush Limbaugh and Charlie Kirk and numerous other far-right figures, that they know how to brush this aside. I mean, JD Vance, when asked about his affiliation with Tucker Carlson, will be like, “He’s my friend.” And that’s it. That’s that.

Okay. So you’re streaming most of the day, you’re reacting to news in real time, and just even by your own admission, you’ve remarked some—I think you said “silly things.” I would say some pretty extreme things along the way.

Recent findings suggest that and I know you’ve walked back past statements. “America deserved 9/11”—how many times have you heard that this season? Quote: “If you cared about Medicare fraud, you’d kill Rick Scott.” You’ve said things that you wish you had said differently. Do you regret anything that you’ve said? Because I think regret is different than “wish I said differently.”.

It’s a tough one. I mean, look, I probably will regret things that I will say in the future as well. It’s virtually impossible for me not to say things—.

It has been revealed that yeah, it is, but it also isn’t because I have apologized and taken back some of the things that I’ve remarked and apologized for how I worded or framed things. But do I regret it? I mean, I feel like I’m stronger as a consequence of all of those experiences at the same time, so I don’t know.

Do you feel like someone in your role has a different responsibility with their words or their public platform than an elected official or even a journalist?

Industry observers note that okay. But you also mentioned that you are a role model.

Yeah, absolutely. It goes back to the space that I occupy and what I try to do with it. Right? I don’t think that I am, at least to my audience or anyone else that’s paying attention, doing anything that’s remotely politically as toxic as the way that the current systems operate.
